raw_comment:
I noticed that for some foods, people thought it was healthy, but nutritionists thought it was unhealthy. For other foods, it was the other way around. For example, only 30% of nutritionists think frozen yogurt is healthy, but 65% of all Americans think it is healthy. But, 90% of nutritionists think quinoa is healthy, but only 55% of all Americans think it is healthy. So, in this graph, the population and nutritionists have opposing opinions. 

I wonder why people have such different opinions than the nutritionists. Maybe because Americans grew up learning what was healthy and what wasn't, and they didn't really try to take a closer look at these foods. Nutritionists spend their time studying food to see what is healthy, so they have more experience about what is healthy. 

You can infer from this graph that some of the foods Americans think are healthy aren't actually very healthy. Or, we think something is unhealthy when it is healthy. This graph goes beyond food because it shows that what we learn isn't always the truth.

raw_comment:
I noticed that a few things, like sushi and quinoa, nutritionists say are pretty healthy, but Americans don't really realize. About 45% of Americans think sushi is healthy, but there's about 80% of nutritionists who think it is... that's 35% more. Also, there's a diagonal line running through the square.
I wonder why Americans don't realize how quinoa and sushi are healthy because, using sushi as my example again, it's just seaweed, rice, fish, and maybe a vegetable (like avocado). I can infer that the diagonal line in the center is what they want everything to be on because that means people are aware of how healthy things are. This would represent a total understanding between Americans and nutritionists.

I think this is because we don't know about everything that these foods are made from. We should eat everything,but in moderation, because these sorts of food could cause various illnesses, like obesity and cancer. the graph also says that wine, and popcorn is healthier than milk. But if wine is had only in moderation, it's okay. Popcorn has lots of butter, and corn which raises blood sugar levels. This  shows that we should really focus on the ingredients when we are buying food, and eat in moderation.

raw_comment:
1. I notice a chart with various food items with the vertical axis detailing the percentage of nutritionists that say that that food is healthy and the horizontal axis detailing the percentage of American consumers saying that that food is healthy. I notice that a lot of the food is on or close to the line going up. I notice that what we refer to as "junk food" is consistently on the lower end of the graph, showing that it is not healthy.

2. I wonder how Americans determine if food is healthy or not. I also wonder how the New York Times got the data for this study. Did the poll random Americans on the street, or found a more educated group of Americans that do not classify as nutritionalists? I also wonder why so many americals think that frozen yogurt is healthy comparted to nutritionalists.

3. The graph compares how nutritionalists and regular Americans view different foods in their nutritional value. I can infer from this graph that sugary foods and drinks are both deemed unhealthy by Americans and nutritionalists. In addition, I can infer that many of the foods that are found to be healthy are natural foods that are directly from a plant or animal and involve no processing.

raw_comment:
I notice that generally the people and the nutritionists of america agree on what foods are good for your health and conversely what is bad for your health. This is a good sign as it points to the fact that people usually have a good grasp on what is healthy or not. 

There are few questions that are brought to mind. I wonder why, if people are so aware of what is good for your body or not, why is America still very obese and unhealthy. This points to the fact that regardless of whether Americas realize that foods are unhealthy, they do not seem to understand the seriousness of eating healthy, or perhaps dont make a special effort to cook at home or go that extra mile to ensure they are eating healthy foods. I believe a survey or a study into various people of different locations and incomes could help point and explain the reasoning behind this behavior. 

The graph gives the story that the public and nutritionists are generally on the same page. This helps point to the underlying problem of how Americans need to act on this knowledge and change there lifestyle, and that education alone will not be enough.

raw_comment: I notice that there is a general positive correlation between the percent of all Americans saying a food is healthy and the percent of nutritionists saying a food is healthy. Some products, such as apples, baked potatoes, and hamburgers, fall right on the line of best fit, while others, such as granola, coconut oil, and frozen yogurt, deviate quite drastically. I wonder what the cause of this deviation could be. My best guess is that it is probably due to the cultural connotations of each of these food items. I also wonder why any nutritionist would consider something like french fries healthy (even though it is less than 10% of nutritionists who say that). I could probably find the answer to this question by searching for nutritionist reviews of products that are generally seen as unhealthy. The story that this graph is telling is a lot of Americans are ignorant about personal health.  The results conveyed by this graph could be used as fuel for social change; it could be used as a call to arms to educate the public about health risks and benefits.

raw_comment:
I notice that many foods that Americans think are unhealthy are also said to be unhealthy by nutritionists. However, some foods that Americans think are unhealthy are actually deemed as healthy by nutritionists and vice versa. This implies that what nutritionists are saying is not getting through to most Americans and that we have many misconceptions about the healthiness of different foods.

I wonder whether the information from this graph has even greater impacts that we do not see directly in the visual. For example, perhaps the graph shows how media has influenced our views on foods and given us the wrong ideas about what seems healthy to us and what is actually healthy according to nutritionists. If we were to pay more attention to the facts, we would be able to make healthier choices about what we eat. I also wonder if there is a reason for these specific foods to be shown on the graph. Are these the most popular foods bought by consumers in America, or perhaps something else entirely?

In the graph, there is a linear regression, showing that most foods are agreed on to an extent to be seen as healthy or unhealthy to both Americans and nutritionists. However, the foods that are not on top of this linear regression can be interpreted as misconceptions of the foods' healthiness. The deeper story to this graph may be that we have found a better way for people to diet and become healthier because when people may have thought they were eating healthily, they actually weren't

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
All American's think more foods are healthy than the nutritionists. The percentage of more of the unhealthy foods, like ice cream are at a higher percentage for all Americans, opposed to nutritionist's thoughts. There aren't many foods that are in the middle, like that are the same percentage of healthy for each group either. The calories also aren't included with the food item.
What do you wonder?
I wonder what the data would be if it was focused on two different groups of people rather than all American's and nutritionists. I also wonder what the data would be, how different it would look if more/different food options were included in the graph. I wonder what it would be like if the number of calories were included with each food item and how that would affect the graph.
What's going on in this graph?
In this graph, certain foods are being displayed to show the thoughts of people on how healthy the food is. All Americans think more food is healthy opposed to nutritionists. The graphs have a different scale for each axis also. There is a wide range of food options shown in the graph, which make the data easier to look at.

raw_comment:
Period 7 Algebra 1

We noticed that regular Americans think most healthier than they actually are (per the nutritionists).  Most foods that are filled with sugar are towards the origin of the graph which implies that we should not be eating much sugary foods.  We need more educated on the nutritional value of foods.  Towards the middle of the graph are more dairy foods which may mean we should limit our dairy.  

We wonder why there a huge gap between healthy and unhealthy food.  Why was there a group of food below the line of best fit?  They seem to be healthy foods but not to nutritionists. 

This graph is trying to tell us that some foods are not as healthy as you think they are.  The graph is comparing the nutritionists views to ours.   Americans need to become more educated with a food's real nutritional value.

raw_comment: This graph seemingly represents the average American citizen's perception of what a healthy food is as compared to what foods nutritionists say are actually healthy. It starts out with the most commonly known unhealthy foods at the bottom of the graph (meaning the majority of Americans are aware those foods are not healthy, according to nutritionists), such as soda, beer, chocolate chip cookies, pizza, french fries, bacon, ice cream, etc. The graph then continues to increase with the amount of foods Americans think are healthy and the amount of nutritionists who agree with said Americans' perceptions. These foods include fruits, wheat instead of white breads, vegetables, nuts, and white meats. What is interesting to note is the smaller section of foods on the bottom right corner of the graph. These include granola, granola bars, coconut oil, and frozen yogurt. This section represents the foods which Americans perceive as being healthy/good for their well-being, but their supposed healthiness has been disputed by nutritionists. What I am curious to know is why/how/when Americans' perceptions of these gray-area foods were pushed so off course.

raw_comment:
I notice that, in general, most of the foods included in this graph fall close to the y = x line, implying that most of Americans' perceptions of what foods are healthy or not coincide with the opinions of nutritionists. I also notice that there are certain clusters that fall both below and above the y = x line. Below, there is a cluster including granola and frozen yogurt while a cluster above includes tofu and quinoa. The cluster of foods below the y = x line includes foods that Americans deem to be more healthy than nutritionists while the cluster above includes foods that nutritionists say are healthier than what Americans believe them to be.

I wonder why there is disagreement among the foods found in the clusters both above and below the y = x line. Why are there different perceptions of the health of these foods when there seems to be agreement among many of the others? One idea I had was that items such as frozen yogurt are heavily marketed as being a healthy alternative or choice which could lead the general public to view them as healthier than they actually are. Meanwhile, foods like quinoa are not marketed as often which may lead Americans to be unaware of their true nutritional merit.

The story this graph is telling is that, in general, Americans as a whole tend to agree with nutritionists when deeming foods healthy or not, yet there are certain groups of food in which nutritionists and Americans do not agree upon which could be a result of marketing.

raw_comment:
Welcome to What’s Going On in This Graph?.   Do you think you eat healthy foods?  Are you eating healthy?  Maybe these are not easy questions to answer.  Take a hard look at the graph.
What do you NOTICE?  What this may imply?
What do you WONDER?  Where could you find the answers to what you wonder?
What’s the STORY this graph tells?  Use what you notice.  What can you infer that is beyond what this graph shows directly?
The questions are intended to build on one another, so try to answer them in order. Start with “I notice” and then “I wonder,” and end with “The story this graph is telling is ….”
And, your personal perspective may relate the graph not only to its statistics, but also science, history, literature, or somewhere else.
Then, read what other students have to say.  Possibly, what they notice and wonder will lead you to other insights about the graph.  Press "reply" to respond to other comments.
 We look forward to reading your discoveries.

It seemed like some of the foods were grouped together with things they go with. Americans feel that frozen yogurt & granola are healthy but the nutritionists don't seem to agree.
